claim: Line 2 'It switched off on purpose': in India a grid-connected rooftop solar inverter is required by law to disconnect from the grid when the grid supply is lost (anti-islanding is mandatory, CEA connectivity regulations 2013, reg. 11(6)).
source_quote: Distributed generation resource operating in parallel with electricity system shall be equipped with the following protective functions to sense abnormal conditions on electricity system and cause the distributed generation resource to be automatically disconnected from electricity system or to prevent the distributed generation resource from being connected to electricity system inappropriately-
note: Central Electricity Authority (Technical Standards for Connectivity of the Distributed Generation Resources) Regulations 2013 (Gazette of India, 30 Sep 2013, File No. 12/X/STD(CONN)/GM/CEA), consolidated by CBIP with the First Amendment of 6 Feb 2019. Applies to every 'generating station feeding electricity into the electricity system at voltage level of below 33 kV' (def. 2(1)(e)), i.e. rooftop solar. The Odisha regulator's net-metering order applies the same CEA standards to rooftop PV: 'The photo voltaic system in the event of fault, voltage or frequency variations must island / disconnect itself within IEC standard on stipulated period' (OERC Case 16/2019, https://www.orierc.org/Orders/2019/C-16-2019.pdf). MNRE's 2017 Compulsory Registration Order makes PV inverters conform to IS 16169 (islanding-prevention test), see S20. No later amendment found on 2026-10-21; CEA's 2026 draft connectivity regulations cover only connections at 33 kV and above (KS&K, https://ksandk.com/md/newsletter/cea-draft-grid-connectivity-standards-2026/). cea.nic.in now shows a login page, so the CBIP copies were used. Tag: [CEA REGULATIONS 2013 | REG. 11(6)].

claim: Line 2 'to protect a lineman's life': the reason for the shutdown is the safety of line workers, who could otherwise touch a line still energised by the solar system.
source_quote: 3. Islanding may create a hazard for utility line-workers or the public by causing a line to remain energized that may be assumed to be disconnected from all energy sources.
note: IEA PVPS Report T5-09 (2002), Bower (Sandia) and Ropp, section 2. It is one of five reasons the report gives (also customer-equipment damage, out-of-phase reclosing and interference with restoration), so on screen do not call it the only reason. The report also notes that crews who follow dead-line rules (test and earth) are protected, so anti-islanding is the backstop. Indian installer SolarSquare gives the same reason: 'This essential safety feature is hard-coded so linemen who repair faulty lines are not exposed to electrocution.' (https://www.solarsquare.in/blog/on-grid-vs-off-grid/, updated 18 Oct 2026).

claim: Line 2 'The sun is still shining. But your fans stop': with no battery, a grid-tie inverter makes no AC from the panels once the grid has failed, so the house gets nothing from its solar in full sun.
source_quote: If the grid fails or is inactive, the inverter will not be able to generate any AC power using PV power.
note: Solis S6-EH1P hybrid user manual (US models), section 4.1.1 'Grid-Tie PV String Inverter' (the hybrid run with no battery). Universal for grid-connected rooftop inverters in India because of the CEA rule (S01, S18).

claim: Line 4: the box the panels connect to is what Indian installers and makers call an 'on-grid inverter', and it is not the home battery inverter (an on-grid system works without a battery).
source_quote: An on-grid inverter has one job: to take the electricity generated by your solar panels and make it ready for use in your home or business.
note: Luminous (Indian inverter maker) on-grid inverter page. Same page: 'An on-grid solar system works without a battery, which keeps the installation simpler'. 'Solar box' is our own nickname.

claim: Line 5: panels give D.C. power, which flows only one way.
source_quote: It’s a device that converts direct current (DC) electricity, which is what a solar panel generates, to alternating current (AC) electricity, which the electrical grid uses. In DC, electricity is maintained at constant voltage in one direction.
note: U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Energy Technologies Office, 'Solar Integration: Inverters and Grid Services Basics'. A panel's DC voltage changes with sunlight, but its direction does not, so 'flows only one way' is right.

claim: Line 6: homes run on A.C., which swings forward and back.
source_quote: In AC, electricity flows in both directions in the circuit as the voltage changes from positive to negative.
note: Same DOE page as S05.

claim: Line 6: India's mains supply runs at 50 Hz (on-screen 50 Hz).
source_quote: The declared frequency of the alternating current (AC) shall be 50 HZ.
note: Meghalaya SERC Supply Code 2012, clause 2.1(1). The CEA DG regulations set the inverter frequency trips around 50 Hz (50.5 Hz / 47.5 Hz, S17) and DISCOM transformer specs are '50 HZ' (WBSEDCL, S15). Tag: [STATE SUPPLY CODE].

claim: Line 6 'fifty full swings every second': 50 Hz means 50 complete forward-and-back cycles per second, so one cycle lasts 20 ms (storyboard HUD 'CYCLE 20 ms').
source_quote: "frequency" means the number of alternating cycles per second expressed in Hertz;
note: CEA DG regulations 2013, def. 2(1)(f). OUR CALCULATION: 1 / 50 = 0.02 s = 20 ms per cycle. A cycle reverses direction twice, so the current changes direction 100 times a second: 'fifty full swings' (forward and back) is right, and 'flips fifty times' would be wrong.

claim: Line 6: the solar box (inverter) turns the panels' D.C. into the A.C. used at the wall socket.
source_quote: "inverter" means a device that changes direct current power into alternating current power;
note: CEA DG regulations 2013, def. 2(1)(j). DOE page (S05) says the same.

claim: Line 7-8: a grid-tied (grid-following) inverter cannot set the A.C. rhythm on its own; it takes its timing from the grid and follows it ('a dancer that only follows the drum').
source_quote: Traditional “grid-following” inverters require an outside signal from the electrical grid to determine when the switching will occur in order to produce a sine wave that can be injected into the power grid. In these systems, the power from the grid provides a signal that the inverter tries to match.
note: DOE page (S05). The inverter does build the wave itself by switching, but it takes the timing from the grid (a phase-locked loop); 'can't make that rhythm on its own' is a fair plain-words version. DOE itself uses a 'dance partners' picture for grid-forming and grid-following inverters. CEA reg. 11(4) exempts inverters from a separate synchronising device 'if the same is inherently built into the inverter'.

claim: Line 8: on a normal day the surplus goes out through the house meter onto the street wire, toward the transformer (net metering export).
source_quote: Yes, Luminous’ on grid solar power system supports net metering, allowing you to export surplus electricity to the grid and earn credits on your electricity bill.
note: CEA 2019 amendment, def. 2(1)(ja): a prosumer 'consumes electricity from the grid and can also inject electricity into the grid, using same point of connection' (CBIP consolidated text). Physics nuance: exported power is mostly used by neighbours on the same street wire and passes up through the pole transformer only when the street makes more than it uses. 'Up to the transformer on the pole' is fine as the path (meter, service wire, street line fed by the transformer); the picture should not imply that all export always reaches the transformer.

claim: Line 9: a power cut can be the electricity board switching off a section of the network (for example for repairs), which is when linemen work on lines they believe are dead.
source_quote: 4. Intentional disconnect for servicing either at a point on the utility or at the service entrance;
note: IEA T5-09 list of conditions that can create an island; it also lists '3. Utility switching of the distribution system and loads;' and faults. The scenario in the VO is one of the listed cases.

claim: Line 10: if the solar box kept pushing after the cut, the dead street wire would be live again (an 'unintended island').
source_quote: "unintended island" means a part of the electricity system which remains energised by one or more distributed generation resource, when such part of the system has been isolated from the remaining part of the electricity system;
note: CEA DG regulations 2013, def. 2(1)(m), Gazette of India 30 Sep 2013, page 7-8. IEA T5-09: 'Islanding is a condition in which a portion of the utility system, which contains both load and generation, is isolated from the remainder of the utility system and continues to operate.'

claim: Line 11: the pole transformer works in reverse: power pushed into its low-voltage side energises its high-voltage side and the line beyond it (back-feed).
source_quote: When current-source inverters are used, and when the switch that disconnects the utility voltage source from the island is on the primary side of the transformer, as shown in Figure 1, the secondary of the transformer will be excited by the output current of the PV inverter.
note: IEA T5-09 section 4.1.3.2. Second, independent source: U.S. OSHRC decision, Secretary of Labor v. Pike Electric, Docket 06-0166 (ALJ, 26 Mar 2007): a homeowner's portable generator back-fed a de-energised three-phase line (normally 'energized at 7,220 volts, phase to ground') through a transformer that 'was not opened, tagged, flagged and grounded', and lineman Adams was electrocuted (S17). HyperPhysics: a transformer can 'raise or lower AC voltages' (http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/magnetic/transf.html).

claim: Line 11: Indian homes are supplied at 230 V single-phase (on-screen 230 V).
source_quote: (i) Single Phase: 230 volts between, a phase and neutral
note: Meghalaya SERC Supply Code 2012, clause 2.1(1)(a); same clause lists 'High Tension (HT) - Three Phase: 11 kV, 22 kV, 33 kV between phases.' Independent: UP Electricity Supply Code 2005, clause 3.1(b): 'Low Tension (LT) - Single Phase: 230 volts between phases and neutral. - Three Phase: 400 volts between phases.' (https://uperc.org/App_File/U-P-ElectricitySupplyCode2005upto12thAmendment-pdf323201825406PM.pdf). Tag: [STATE SUPPLY CODES].

claim: Line 11: 'Your two hundred and thirty volts... becomes about eleven thousand volts': the street's pole transformer is an 11 kV / 433 V unit, so 230 V fed back into it appears at about 11,000 V on the high-voltage line (on-screen 11,000 V).
source_quote: supply & delivery of three phase 50 HZ, 11/ 0.433 KV, Delta/Star, Vector Group Dyn11, two winding, oil immersed naturally Oil & Air cooled
note: WBSEDCL technical specification, 315 kVA '3 PHASE POLE MOUNTED' distribution transformer, voltage ratio '11000 / 433 V'. OUR CALCULATION: each low-voltage winding is 433 / 1.732 = 250 V, each high-voltage winding 11,000 V, ratio 44. 230 V x 44 = 10,120 V; 250 V x 44 = 11,000 V. 'About eleven thousand volts' is fair (within about 8%) and 11 kV is the line's rating. ON-SCREEN CAUTION: show '≈ 11,000 V' or '11 kV LINE'; a counter that lands exactly on 11,000 from 230 overstates it slightly.

claim: Line 11 'On a wire the lineman thinks is switched off': back-fed power can energise a line that crews treat as dead and kill a line worker.
source_quote: The homeowner had connected a portable generator to the house’s circuitry which caused electrical energy to backfeed to the line Adams was splicing, energizing it. Adams was electrocuted when he cut the line
note: OSHRC Docket 06-0166 (Pike Electric), findings of fact. Same record: 'Pike was treating the power lines as de-energized because Alabama Power Company had opened the switches inside the substation'. IEA T5-09 reason 3 (S02) states the same hazard in general terms.

claim: Line 12: 'If the beat goes missing, or the voltage starts changing, it switches itself off... click': the inverter must trip on abnormal voltage or frequency and open its grid relay.
source_quote: over and under voltage trip functions if voltage reaches above 110% or below 80% respectively with a clearing time upto two seconds; however, appropriate licensee may prescribe a narrower range of voltage for the purpose.
note: CEA reg. 11(6)(a). Reg. 11(6)(b): 'over and under frequency trip functions, if frequency reaches 50.5 Hz and below 47.5 Hz with a clearing time upto 0.2 seconds'. IEA T5-09 calls these OVP/UVP and OFP/UFP (passive detection). The 'click' is the grid relay opening (Solis manual: 'it automatically opens the relay between itself and the grid'; Deye on-grid manual fault list: 'Check relays and AC voltage of relays.'). HUD CAUTION: India's over-frequency trip is 50.5 Hz (a DISCOM may set it narrower), so any 'TRIP' frequency on screen must be 50.5 Hz or lower, never 50.6 or 50.7 Hz.

claim: Line 12: 'Safety rules say it must switch off within two seconds': the Indian rule itself sets two seconds for an island (on-screen ≤ 2 s).
source_quote: a function to prevent the distributed generation resource from contributing to the formation of an unintended island, and cease to energise the electricity system within two seconds of the formation of an unintended Island.
note: Gazette of India Extraordinary, Part III Sec. 4, 30 Sep 2013, page 10, CEA reg. 11(6)(e); unchanged by the 2019 amendment (CBIP consolidated text). The Indian rule states exactly two seconds, so 'Safety rules' can stay (no change to 'international safety standards' needed). 'Cease to energise' = stop feeding power = 'switch off'. Two seconds is the maximum; real inverters usually trip sooner (not claimed). Tag: [CEA REG. 11(6)(e) | IEEE 1547 | IS 16169], CEA first for Indian viewers.

claim: Line 12 (same two seconds): the international standard IEEE 1547-2018 also sets two seconds.
source_quote: For an unintentional island in which the DER energizes a portion of the Area EPS through the PCC, the DER shall detect the island, cease to energize the Area EPS, and trip within 2 s of the formation of an island.
note: Unitil / Massachusetts TSRG 'Default IEEE 1547-2018 Setting Requirements' (9 May 2022), quoting IEEE 1547-2018 as amended by 1547a-2020, Clause 8.1.1. Independent: AEP 'DER Technical Interconnection and Interoperability Requirements' (effective 1 Feb 2024), section 7.1: 'As required by IEEE Std 1547™-2018 Clause 8.1, ... trip within 2.0 seconds of the formation of the island.' (https://docs.aep.com/docs/requiredpostings/DERInterconnectionRequirements_UpdatedRev3_final_02-01-2024.pdf).

claim: Line 12 (same two seconds): the inverter islanding test IS 16169 / IEC 62116, compulsory for PV inverters sold in India, passes an inverter only if it stops within 2 s.
source_quote: An EUT is considered to comply with the requirements for islanding protection when each case of recorded run-on time is less than 2 s or meets the requirements of local codes.
note: BIS test report format for IS 16169:2019 / IEC 62116:2014, clause 6.2 (bis.gov.in). Compulsory: pv magazine India, 10 Apr 2019 (Uma Gupta): 'The Solar Photovoltaics Systems, Devices and Components Goods (Requirements for Compulsory Registration) Order 2017 prohibits sales, import or distribution of goods that do not conform to specified Indian standards—IS 16221 (Part 2): 2015 and IS 16169:2014 in the case of PV inverters.' (https://www.pv-magazine-india.com/2019/04/10/mnre-issues-guidelines-for-approval-of-solar-inverters/). IS 16221 (Part 2) is the inverter safety standard ('Safety of Power Converters for use in Solar Photovoltaic Power Systems', same article), not the islanding test.

claim: Line 13 (mechanism): when the power used on the cut-off section exactly matches the solar feeding it, the cut changes neither voltage nor frequency, so the ordinary voltage and frequency checks cannot see it.
source_quote: If ∆P = ∆Q = 0 when the utility disconnects or opens, there will be insufficient change in the amplitude or frequency of va to activate any of the standard over/under voltage or frequency protection devices. This corresponds to a case in which the PV (inverter output) power production is matched to the load power requirement, and the load has a unity power factor at the line frequency.
note: IEA T5-09 section 4.1.1.5. The same report: passive protection alone is 'generally considered to be insufficient anti-islanding protection'. IS 16169 / IEC 62116 tests exactly this case: 'The test uses an RLC load, resonant at the EUT nominal frequency (50 Hz or 60 Hz) and matched to the EUT output power.' (BIS TRF, clause 6.1). The VO leaves out the reactive-power part of the match; acceptable simplification.

claim: Line 13 VO wording: 'Say your house is using exactly what the panels make. Then the power cut changes nothing — the box can't feel it.' (In this film the cut switches off the whole street, line 9.)
source_quote: The NDZ is the range of local loads (that is, loads inside the potential island) for which the islanding prevention method under consideration can be made to fail to detect islanding.
note: WRONG AS WORDED. The balance that hides a cut is between everything left on the cut-off section and all the solar feeding it (IEA: ΔP and ΔQ are the power flowing through the switch that opened). Line 9 has the board switch off the whole street, so the neighbours' loads stay wired to your solar box after the cut. If only your house is balanced, their fans and lights pull the voltage down at once (IEA: 'If ∆P≠0, the amplitude of va will change, and the OVP/UVP can detect the change'), and the ordinary voltage check trips the box: no tricky case. FIX (re-record one sentence, same voice and settings): 'Say your whole street is using exactly what the solar panels make.' Then keep 'Then the power cut changes nothing — the box can't feel it.' The fixed vo.txt copy passes scripts/spoken_english_check.py (558 words). Picture: the balance scale must weigh the street's use against all the panels' output, with zero flow at the transformer, not one house.

claim: Lines 14-16: the box plays 'a little off-beat on purpose'; with the grid present the frequency is held, without it the frequency keeps drifting until the frequency trip switches the box off (active anti-islanding).
source_quote: In this method, the waveform of the current injected into node “a” by the PV inverter is slightly distorted such that there is a continuous trend to change the frequency. When connected to the utility it is impossible to change the frequency.
note: IEA T5-09 section 4.2.4 (Frequency Bias / Active Frequency Drift). Same section: 'When disconnected from the utility, the frequency of va is forced to drift up or down' and 'This process continues until the frequency has drifted far enough from ω0 to be detected by the over/under frequency protection (OFP/UFP).' Real products do this: Eastups EA-series grid-tie inverter manual, 'Anti-islanding protection: Shifting the frequency of the inverter away from nominal conditions in the absence of a reference frequency (frequency shift)' (https://en.eastups.com/u/cms/en/202009/15095607fk1j.pdf). Other inverters use other active tests (impedance or reactive-power nudges), so the film shows one common method; HUD values ILLUSTRATIVE with the trip line at 50.5 Hz (S18).

claim: Line 17 'Once the box is off... Nothing comes out': with the inverter off, the panel circuit is open; the voltage is at its maximum but no current flows, so the panels deliver zero power (P = V x I).
source_quote: the open circuit voltage (Voc) value occurs at the bottom right side of the curve. At this point, the voltage is at its maximum, and current flow is zero.
note: EC&M, 'The Highs and Lows of Photovoltaic System Calculations', Mayfield (Renewable Energy Associates), 23 Jul 2012. HyperPhysics: 'P = VI Power = Voltage x Current' (http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/electric/elepow.html). Adani module manual: 'A solar array generates DC electricity when sunlight falls on the modules and the inverter is in active mode.' On-screen 'V = Voc · I = 0 A · P = 0 W' is correct.

claim: Line 18 'The sunlight still lands and just turns into heat — your panels are built for that': a module left at open circuit in sun runs only a few degrees warmer than a working one, well inside its rated range.
source_quote: Results showed the short-circuited module's temperature was 6.90 °C higher, and the open-circuited module's temperature was 3.67 °C higher than the MPP module.
note: Osama, Tina, Gagliano, Jiménez-Castillo, Muñoz-Rodríguez, Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells 287 (2025) 113625, doi 10.1016/j.solmat.2025.113625 (4-month outdoor test, Jaén, Spain). Rated range: Adani installation manual 'Operating temperature -40°C to +85°C'. The industry NOCT rating is itself measured on 'open circuited cells in a module' (Sinovoltaics, https://sinovoltaics.com/learning-center/quality/normal-operating-cell-temperature-noct-definition-noct-definition/). 'Just turns into heat' is a fair simplification (some light is reflected). Covers outage-length periods, not months of disconnection. If a number is shown: '+3.7 °C (ONE STUDY)'.

claim: Line 18 'But the panel wires still have voltage in them': lit panels are live even when nothing is connected or the inverter is off.
source_quote: PV module connectors pass direct current (DC) when exposed to sunlight or other light sources. Contact with electrically active parts of the module, such as terminals, can result in injury or death, irrespective of whether or not the module and the other electrical equipment have been connected.
note: DMEGC module installation manual (Ver 202301). EC&M (S25): 'it is safe to assume that if there is ambient light, the PV module has the ability to produce its full rated voltage.' Adani manual: 'On direct exposure to Sunlight, PV module produces electricity, which can result in electric shock'. No panel-voltage number on screen unless sourced; 'STILL LIVE' is right.

claim: Line 18 'So don't touch them yourself — leave that to a trained person'.
source_quote: It is recommended that all the solar module, module array and the DC combiner box should be handled by only trained person.
note: Adani Solar PV module installation manual MSEL/MSPVL/IM02/2024. DMEGC manual: 'The installation and handling of PV modules require professional skills and should only be performed by qualified professionals.'

claim: Line 19: to keep fans running in a power cut you need a different box, a hybrid inverter, which works with the grid and with a battery.
source_quote: Hybrid inverters compatible with both solar modules and energy storage systems have been added
note: Mercom India, 28 Nov 2025 (Odisha net-metering rules now allow hybrid inverters). Solis S6 hybrid manual: 'The S6 hybrid is capable of providing AC power to home loads using PV and battery power in the event of a grid failure. This is known as backup power.' Battery: the same hybrid without a battery makes no AC in an outage (S03), so 'with a battery' is the right definition. Other routes exist (an off-grid system, or a battery inverter AC-coupled beside the existing on-grid box, which the Solis manual also describes), but each still needs a battery-capable inverter, so 'a different box' holds. Not misleading.

claim: Line 20: 'When the grid dies, a switch inside it first cuts your house off from the street. Then the battery becomes the drummer, and the panels dance again.'
source_quote: When the inverter senses that the grid power has been lost, it automatically opens the relay between itself and the grid. It keeps the relay closed to the backup, allowing it to supply AC power to the home loads as long as power is available.
note: Solis S6-EH1P manual, section 4.4. Independent: Sungrow 3-phase Hybrid backup factsheet (2021): 'In case of a grid failure the bypass switch inside the 3-phase Hybrid opens and all loads connected to the backup port will get a seamless transition into backup mode. Only loads not connected to the backup port experience the black out.' and 'Within less than 20 ms a bypass switch will open and up to 9.9 kW of loads connected to the backup port will be supplied by the battery and PV.' CAVEAT: only the circuits wired to the backup output (e.g. fans and lights) are cut off from the street and powered; the rest of the house stays dark unless the installer wires the whole house to backup. Picture: show the backed-up fans coming back, not every appliance. Switchover time on screen only with a model label (e.g. '< 20 MS · SUNGROW 3-PHASE'), or leave it out.

claim: Line 20 'the battery becomes the drummer': in backup mode the battery-fed inverter makes its own A.C. timing (grid-forming) instead of following the grid.
source_quote: More advanced grid-forming inverters can generate the signal themselves.
note: DOE page (S05). Same page: 'Solar-plus–battery storage systems rely on advanced inverters to operate without any support from the grid in case of outages, if they are designed to do so.' Strictly the hybrid inverter, running on the battery, sets the beat; the analogy is fine.

claim: Line 21: 'A normal on-grid solar box, with no battery, has to go silent when the grid goes. That's by design.'
source_quote: a voltage and frequency sensing and time-delay function to prevent the distributed generation resource from energising a de-energised circuit and to prevent the distributed generation resource from reconnecting with electricity system unless voltage and frequency is within the prescribed limits and are stable for at least sixty seconds; and
note: CEA reg. 11(6)(d), with 11(6)(e) (S19). It also means the box waits for at least sixty seconds of stable grid before it restarts (useful if the film ever shows the return). Solis no-battery behaviour: S03.

claim: Line 22 'If anyone offers to switch off this safety': some inverters expose an anti-islanding on/off setting, so an installer could switch it off; doing so breaks the CEA rule.
source_quote: Island: Anti-islanding protection
note: Deye SUN-(1-4)K-G04P1-EU on-grid inverter manual (June 2026): the 'Island' item (ON/OFF) sits in the password-protected running-parameter menu. Switching it off breaks CEA reg. 11(6)(e), and CEA reg. 15(2) (2019 amendment): 'The user may be disconnected from the grid by the licensee for non-compliance of any provision of these regulations'. Never show the real menu or steps.

claim: Line 22 'Because the lineman fixing your street is the one who gets the shock': back-fed power from a customer's inverter has killed a lineman in India, even after he had switched off and earthed the line.
source_quote: He said, Zambaulikar had taken all the precautions before embarking on his task such as putting off the main supply and also temporarily earthing it but the 'back field' supply to the neutral line from the Fitness Factory's inverter did him in.
note: The Goan, 20 Apr 2024, quoting Goa's Chief Electrical Engineer Stephen Fernandes (a commercial battery inverter with no earthing, not rooftop solar, but the same back-feed hazard). U.S. case: OSHRC 06-0166 (S17). It is a risk, not a certainty (crews also test and earth lines, IEA T5-09), but the VO's line names the person at risk and is acceptable.
